doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Too Many People, clarinet overdubs and openness to players
summary: John Ellis added clarinet to the track; Sidran leaves room for players like Phil Woods to change direction.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: How about this song “Too Many People, Nothing to Say.” There’s this fabulous rhythmic hook. I tried to write it down, I’m not sure I got it, it was like [scats].
Yeah. That little ghost note in there.
Yeah, that’s it. That’s exactly right.
How did the clarinets come to pass? Where does that come from? Do you have people who make suggestions? Is that all you?

No. John Ellis, who played clarinet, I’ve been recording and playing gigs with him, I don’t know maybe for ten years now. And he’s got this real fresh open sound. And that was overdubbed, I mean we had that track and then you’re absolutely right to say that whole track is built on that ghost note. And the lyrics — “Too many people/Got nothing to say/It’s underhanded but I can understand it.” It was just play. It was fun. And I gave a copy of that track to Ellis. Because he had worked — I mean it was kind of an R&B approach. And he came back with that really modern clarinet thing. I mean it was totally unexpected to me which actually gets to a point in how I approach recording, which is a lot of people know exactly what they want, and they’ll tell you what they want, and they’ll tell you if you’re not doing it right. I don’t do that. My whole thing is about © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

people. If I like somebody’s approach and I like them as a player I’m open to what they come up with that is probably more interesting than what I’m looking for. Because what I’m looking for is just one — there’s no right part really, to me. You know a lot of things could work. So often on the recordings that I’ve made I’ll have something in mind and then somebody like Phil Woods will come along and just change the entire direction of what I imagined, and it’s Phil Woods, well of course. You know that’s why he’s Phil Woods and that’s why you hire him. And that’s what that clarinet part was.
